speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

In the fall of 1916 the Government established rural mail delivery from Glenelm in the township of Elgin, and closed some of the post offices. As a result of the change a number of families, a3 I represented to the department on the 2nd of January this year, living along the first concession of Elgin, which is the main road running through the whole county of Huntingdon, were deprived of their post office and also of rural mail delivery. They think it most unfair that they should not be served toy rural mail delivery now that the post office at Powerscourt has been closed. I -should like a statement from the minister as to whether he proposes to give these f-armers the service they are entitled to.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: _ The Deputy Minister explains to me that'the parties living along this mile of road are within half a mile of a rural mail route on either side of them, and I understand that under the regulations if the route is -within a mile that is * all that can properly be expected. Under these ,circum-stan-c-es, unless there is some - special reason why the rule should be departed from, there -would hardly seem to toe justification for providing for the carrying of mail between the two routes I have referred to. I understand that the parties complaining desire a -connecting route, so to -speak, between the two present existing routes, -and I am informed that none of them are more than -half a mile distant from one or other of the existing rural mail routes.

What I want to make clear is that this mile of road deprived _ of rural mail service is the main road running through the whole county of Huntingdon from Hem-min-gford to Dundee. The rural route is run up a side line. Wnat I want from the minister is a direct statement whether the department will take into consideration the rights of the families living along this mile of main ro-ad.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not like to say absolutely that I will not take into consideration anything that the hon. member
represents, but I am informed by the Deputy Minister that to meet the wishes of those on whose behalf he is speaking would involve a departure from the general system of laying but the mail routes, which he assures me has been followed in laying out the routes in this particular section. The hon. member speaks about the rights of the people who live on this strip of road. I do not understand that everybody has a right to have a mail route pass his front door. There has to be some limit as to distance, and I am informed that the parties in question are well within what is considered under the general rule to be such a distance from a mail route as to give rise to no ground for complaint. If I understand the hon. member correctly the basis of his claim that the mail route ought to follow this road, is that it forms part of the main road running through the county of Huntingdon. On the other hand it is represented to me that the present disposition of the mail routes in that section is -more generally convenient to the public than if one of the routes were to be sacrificed, so that the mail could be carried along this strip of road. However, I shall be glad to look into the matter to get a clearer comprehension of it myself, and to see whether there is reasonable ground for complaint.

This matter has been before the department since last January, and I wrote the Deputy Postmaster General that I would bring it up again when the Post Office estimates were under consideration. Has the ins-pect-or reported against giving these people this service?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Deputy Minister informs me that he is not in a position to speak positively, but he believes there, must be a report from the inspector on the subject. I cannot undertake to say off-hand whether this service will be granted, nor would I give an absolute refusal, but I shall certainly look into the matter and if it appears that there is a grievance I shall be glad to try and find a remedy.

Will the minister give us the assurance that he will have another report made on the matter? This is a matter which has been before the department since early in January, and complaint was filed by the secretary-treasurer of the municipality, and representations have been made by people who live there, and who should know, that the route could have

been laid out more economically for the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I certainly shall get the facts and give them my best consideration.
In offices such as Almonte, Carleton Place, Clayton, Appleton, Paltenham, etc.,__
These are all towns in the county I have the honour to represent.

Does the department
undertake of its own volition to institute a rural mail service in a particular locality, or ,does it wait until the people ask for.it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand as a general rule-in fact, I may almost say as an absolute rule-it is done upon the request of the parties interested.

Following the question of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), I would like to ask if the department has organized rural mail delivery along routes where two-thirds of the people have protested against it and have stated they wei'e better satisfied with their post office service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand from the deputy minister that there have been rural mail deliveries established after some portions of the people along the routes had objected to its being done. They were established because it was found that the service could be more economically and advantageously carried out by the establishment of the routes, and because it appeared that the people who objected did so through caprice. There have been cases where rural routes have been established although the desire of a portion of the people was to adhere to the post office system, but I am told that was done because it was believed to be in the best interests of the locality.
I understand that unless one-half of the people interested purchase the boxes the route is not established, and the fact that the route is established indicates at all events the consent of at least one-half the persons interested.

I have a communication from a postmaster in the county I have the honour to represent, which I would like to place before the committee. The member for St. Antoine division (Sir Herbert Ames) drew attention to the small salaries paid the city postmasters. This communication deals with the very small salaries paid to postmasters in towns and villages, and if the statements made are correct, I think the poorest paid officials in the employ of the Government are the postmasters in the towns, villages and rural municipalities. This communication is headed, "Compensation of Country Postmasters." It says:
After Confederation the scale of commission on which postmasters' salaries was fixed 
-was torty per cent on first $800 of postal revenue, and twenty-five per cent on amount of revenue in excess of $800.
Some years ago (probably ten or fifteen) it was felt that this scale ought to be made more favourable to the postmasters, so a new scale was adopted under which the postmaster received fifty per cent on first one- thousand dollars of postal revenue and thirty per cent on ^ amount of revenue in excess of $1,000. This scale was used, without any suggestion that the postmasters were being overpaid, until the introduction of the war tax on letters. Then the' department thought that the increased revenue by reason of war stamps would give the postmasters too much on that scale. So, some Inside Service man who finds he cannot live on his 1914 salary, figured that the proper thing was to go back to the Confederation scale of forty per cent to $800, and twenty-five per cent on excess above $800, and this has been done. Please note that the postage rates to-day (including war stamps) are still lower than at Confederation; please note that the cost of living to-day is about double what it was at Confederation; please note that the country postmaster does a much greater volume of work to-day which does not produce revenue to the credit of his office than he ever did; and please note that the scale on which the country postmaster is being paid to-day is the same as at Confederation.
I say that the country postmaster does a greater volume of work to-day which does not produce revenue to the credit of his office, than he ever did. The enormous increase in the circulation of daily newspapers of late years, and especially since extension of rural mail system, involves a burden of daily work, 310 days in the year, which does not increase his office revenue by a cent, and the extension of the parcel post system has had the effect of bringing into his office for distribution the departmental store shipments which pay their postage to the city officers ; and his work in the distribution of parcels, which produces no revenue in his office, is out of all proportion to what he collects on parcels despatched from his office.
A single illustration will show the weakness and shortsightedness of the action taken in pitchforking us back into the old Confederation scale. Take Pakenham post office as an example. I have not the exact figures, but approximately the postal revenue used to be about $1,000, which gave the postmaster a salary of $500 a year under the old higher scale. In order that he may get a salary of $500 under the present scale, he has to increase his office revenue to $1,520, and he can then meet the increased cost of living' out of the savings he has laid aside out of his salary in previous years.
Does he have to employ an assistant?

I will come to that a little later on. (Reading):
It was quite right that the scale should be modified to make adjustments for the war

stamp addition to revenue, but the rule-of-thumb way they jumped at the thing was inexcusable. Confidentially, I may say-
-and this is the part to which I want to draw the attention of the Acting Postmaster General-
But, it is confidential.

It will work out all right.
-Confidentially I may say that my own salary warrant is $214 per month, out of which I pay three assistants. I have had girls in my employ, who are now in the Civil Service. Those in this post office are just as intelligent and industrious and work longer hours. I give full time to the work myself.
$214 per month means $2,568 per year, and allowing, say, $1,200 salary for himself, there is the enormous sum of $1,368 to pay three assistants. So I think I was justified in saying that the poorest paid officials of the Government are in the Post Office Department. There is no doubt as to the truth of what this postmaster says with reference to the increased work devolving upon them on account of the rural mail and parcel post. They get little or nothing from the sale of postage stamps for parcel post as the parcels are all sent from the cities into the towns and villages. They have to handle all the parcels and get no extra revenue. The same thing applies to the mail going out into the rural districts. It has increased very materially. If there is any department of the Government that needs special care it is the post offices in towns, villages and rural districts.
I have been repeatedly asked, but have been unable to explain, the difference in postage on a parcel to a Canadian soldier in England and in France. The rate from Canada to England is the same as the ordinary parcel post rate before the war, 12 cents per pound. To the Canadian soldier in France or Belgium, the postage on a three-pound parcel is 24 cents. The same parcel to a soldier in England would cost 36 cents. Can the Postmaster General explain why the rate to England is exactly 50 per cent higher than to France or Belgium?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the convention with regard to the postal rate to France and Belgium, Canada receives a certain portion of the postal rates for parcels transmitted to those two countries, and to her own soldiers Canada has thrown off ner part. That makes the< rate cheaper to these countries. The rates between England and Canada are adjusted by arrangement between these two countries. The deputy informs me that although negotiations have been attempted
looking to some arrangement on the subject, nothing has yet been concluded. I have no doubt they have bigger things to attend to over there.
As to the remuneration to country postmasters, I certainly must concede that my hon. friend's correspondent writes a forcible letter. It is exceeded in cogency only by the arguments of the hon. gentlemen in support of it. The subject has been engaging the attention of the department recently. We have had representations by a number of postmasters and an intimation of what they considered would be the proper way to deal with the question. I do not know whether we shall toe able to do quite what they suggest, but I do hope we shall be able to do .something in the direction of improving the condition.

What is minimum paid
to country postmasters?
(Mr. DOHERTY: $50.

We all remember when
the minimum was $10 a year. There has bean a great change in fifteen or sixteen years.

May I add a word on behalf of rural mail carriers? The current impression through some articles that have *appeared in the press is that the carrying of the rural mail is not a matter of contract and that the Government could either increase or reduce the remuneration of the rural mail carrier without any regard to any contract, that the whole thing rested entirely with the Postmaster General. Of course the rural mail carrier takes a contract to carry mail at a certain price for a certain term of years and he gets that amount of money. He cannot secure an increase without the route being once more put up to tender. Since many of the existing contracts were entered into, a great deal of additional work has been .imposed on the carriers through the parcel post system; there has been an increase of perhaps 40 per cent or 50 .per cent. There is general dissatisfaction among the carriers, who think they should get .something additional for this work. It would 'be invidious to grant an additional sum to any special route, but owing to the increased cost of living and the additional cost of carrying the mail, the higher price of horse feed, etc., and the higher cost of labour, if any is employed, there is not much profit left for the rural mail carrier to-day, and I think the department would be justified in giving an increase of 10 or 15 per cent to all rural mail carriers. The rural mail system probably

pays the country as well as the old system of having little country post offices with couriers carrying the mail to these offices a,nd postmasters paid for attending to the offices. I wish to put in a special plea for the country mail carrier. I trust the minister will remember it and that when the Supplementary Estimates come down we shall find that the rural mail carriers will receive a flat increase of 10 per cent or 15 per cent. That should be done in justice to these men, owing to the great increase in their work through the establishment of the parcels post system. The Government must have a very large increase in revenue from parcel post. The figures have not bfeen given to the House. Are they available?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am told there is not
any separate accounting.
How much is the general increase in post office revenue from the sale of stamps since the parcel post sy.s-tem was instituted? Will it be 20 per cent?
You will have to eliminate the war tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed it is safe
You will have to eliminate tne war tax.

I think five per cent of
that increase should go to the rural staff. A number of these local carriers were paid for handling local express. A woman, for instance, would give a man a parcel of eggs and perhaps give him ten cents, but now that is all done away with, and the carriers receive nothing in that way. I think the Government should increase the pay of these men at least 10 per cent. Referring to the soldiers, I was on the Board of Inquiry on the postal question in England and I gained some knowledge there. I ascertained that the British Government handles all the mail to France free. I will be corrected if I am wrong. Therefore, the French Government gives us nothing, as the statement was made. When a parcel is sent from here to a boy in France, it goes to England first, and from there to France., It goes from England to France free, there being one consideration, namely, that that parcel virtually becomes military property the moment it leaves England. If a mother sends a pair of socks to her boy in France, it -goes to England and from England to France, and if the boy happens to be killed or wounded in France, the parcel is expropriated by the military authorities in France, and those socks

go into, a general fund with other articles, the idea, being that it is not fair that these parcels should be returned, but that some use should be made of them at the front. Every mother in England who sends a parcel to her boy knows that that is the rule. I do not think the Canadian women know, and notice of that fact should be given. I might say, also, that all the mail from Canada is handled free by England, and I cannot understand the Postmaster General putting up a story to the effect that he had to pay a large sum for that postage over there. I do not think we have to pay anything for it. That is my own opinion, formed from what I ascertained over there.
When did they put up that story?

The statement was made last year, and repeated again to-night. I think a certain weight of parcel should be permitted to be sent to the soldiers at the front by the mothers in Canada without any postage, as is the practice in England.
Mr.,MARCIL: How about letters?
I would not make that applicable to letters, because the girls would write too many lettei' to the boys at the front.
I asked about that, and they said the Union Postal Regulations were against it.

That is a fallacy. All those regulations fail in time of war. A soldier in the field writes his letter. It is franked by his officer and the letters pass through France, and through the British post office, and come here, and the Post Office Department here places a stamp on them; I do not know why.
I got a letter from the front bearing two Canadian stamps.

They are put on by the postal authorities here. I think the postal regulations, as far as letters and parcels sent to England and France are concerned, require revision. I do not want to attach any blame, but I think the people in this country have been mulcted in large sums for postage on letters to their boys in England, which sums they are not entitled to pay, and that has been an added source of revenue to the department here. The people understood the money had to be paid to England, which I do not think is a fact. I think we would be justified in making some change in the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to question the accuracy of what has been said, but I am informed by the deputy minister that on the cost on parcels from here to France, Canada gets absolutely nothing. With Tegard to parcel post, the rate stands as it stood before the war.
England carries free for us? Mr. DOHERTY: Yes.
Why do we have to pay large sums of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose we could stop charging anything at all, but England will not consent, or has not as yet consented, to the collection u\)on her side, and ft is a matter of arrangement between the two countries.

The minister does not
seem to understand. There is a postal union between the various countries, and under that union each country carries the other's mail free. I speak subject to correction. When we send parcels to France, when they reach England they carry them free. When there is no charge for carrying parcels in England, why do we not follow suit and make no charge? Why do we collect a revenue on parcels here and let the people think we have to pay the money to England? I do not see any items in the Public Accounts showing that there is anything paid for that.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say it costs less to send from Canada to France than it does to send to England? .
Yes.

I understood that was the case. The mother- of two boys, who happened to be very closely connected with myself, told me that in respect of one boy who was in France, the postage was less than it was to her boy in England, both sons serving in the expeditionary force. That seemed to me pretty strange, and certainly it requires explanation. I could not believe it to be true, but my hon. friend from West Simcoe corroborates the statement?
Yes.
What is the reason for that?

There is no charge on these parcels once they land in England, whether they go to England or France, but we are
making a charge on this end, on the understanding that there is a charge on the other end. There is no such chafge. If there is no charge in England, there should be no charge here. I claim the people are paying all that postage to the department here, thinking they have to pay large sums to send things to England and France.
It would look as though somebody ought to study this matter.

I have not heard an explanation yet, and having gone into the matter a little bit, and having been, interested in the matter over there, I ascertained that there was no charge for parcels in England. I went into the matter wihen I was over there and I was given'to understand that there was no chargfe for parcels on the other side. I cannot understand, therefore, why this country is charging for carrying those parcels from inland villages, towns and cities to the coast.
I think it is only fair that a more lucid explanation of the whole matter should be given. If the thing is justified by the old regulations of the Postal Union, then those regulations should be abrogated during the war. Surely Canada can carry parcels for her hoys free if England and France are willing to carry them free.
Mr. LEVI THOMSON': If the hon. member i-3 right, it is an outrage that we should have to pay more for the carriage of parcels to our hoys when they are in England than we have to pay when they are in France. When sending parcels to my boy,
I have often wondered why I had to pay nfore when he was in England than I had to pay when he was in France.

I should like to see the
item in the public accounts showing that we paid for the carriage of these parcels in Epgland and in France; then I would be satisfied that the information which I obtained from different general post offices in England at the beginning of the war was wrong. As .soon as the parcel reached Liverpool it was carried free to London and then sent free to the soldieT in France or wherever he happened to he, no charge being made to the Canadian Government. Indeed, the parcels were handled almost entirely by he Canadian officers over there; they hardly ever went into English hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My information is thaT there are matters in connection with this which it has not been considered desirable
3b46

or proper to explain to the public. But I am in a position to say that whatever may be the reason of it, it does not depend on action which Canada would be free, independently of her contract in the Postal Union arrangement with the Mother Country, to alter. As the matter has been put forward, I shall inquire whether I am at liberty to give an explanation or not. There is an absolutely clear and settled explanation, I am told, making it clear why Canada cannot control the' matter. X cannot say more at the present moment.
This matter is of very great interest to the mothers of the boys who are at the front.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is, and when I am at liberty to do so, I shall explain.

We have heard a great many times during this war that there are all kinds of subjects upon which no information can be given to this Parliament.
I think that the sooner we have a secret session of the House of Commons in order to get some information upon these questions, the better. They have had secret sessions of Parliament in England, as well as in France. Although this country has ' been engaged in the war for nearly three years, not one particle of what may be called secret and important information has been given to this House. This House has never received any information except what has been given to the gen-10 p.m. eral public. I think that the minister ought to let this item stand and get the information, or else give to the committee a satisfactory reason why he does not give us the information now. It is difficult to comprehend why people sending parcels to their boys in England should be obliged to pay more than they pay on parcels going to their boys when they are in France. The minister' says there is a perfectly good reason; well, if there is, I think that Parliament ought to know it.
I can see no reason why it would not be quite right to communicate the information to Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman attaches too great weight to what I said. As to the suggestion that there should be a secret session of Parliament,
I shall be happy to communicate that to the Prime Minister. The hon. gentleman would hardly expect me to undertake to
~f-
The minister is a very important member of the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the hon.
gentleman's appreciation of my importance. I 'Shall be absolutely frank; I do not understand the explanation of the deputy minister, beyond that he does assure me that there is a reason that interferes with our independent action-interferes for the moment, at all events, with my going into the explanation. Perhaps the best reason . why I cannot explain at the present moment is that I do not myself grasp what the reason is.
Perhaps the minister who has been on military service can tell us.

Will (the minister explain why stamps are put on letters sent to Canada by the boys at the front? I have received censored letters from the front upon which Canadian stamps were placed, evidently in Ottawa. Why should this be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That costs nobody
anything, and is to facilitate distribution. Otherwise we would have to have some kind of franking system.

I suppose that adds
something to the apparent revenues of the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The stamps are handed out gratuitously; how could that figure as revenue? That is as difficult to understand as the other explanation. Indeed, if they were charged up, they would help to make a deficit. Whatever the cost of these stamps is, we get nothing back for it. I do not know whether you can trace that loss or not. However, that is the only method of enabling the soldiers' letters to be distributed free without their being held up for lack of postage. The method is the simplest and costs nobody anything.
Why not stamp the letters " free."?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If it is thought that the revenues of the country will be increased or any good purpose be served by stamping the word "free" upon the letters instead of affixing a stamp, which has so far been found the most convenient method, of course we shall be glad to do it. I cannot, however, see what advantage would be in that. I might have a calculation made as to how much these postage stamps cost the country and what difference in cost would be involved in buying a rubber stamp, paying for the ink, and stamping "free" upon the envelope. If there is any differ-

enee in favour of the latter method we might adopt it. I must say, however, that I am doubtful whether there would be any advantage in departing from our present method.

How does the placing of a stamp on a letter from the front at St. John or Halifax expedite the delivery of a letter to an internal point in Canada? As the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) says, the letter is franked in France.
The censor's stamp is the frank.

When I mail a letter in the House of Commons with my frank on it, any hon. friend does not have to put a stamp on it in order to ensure safe delivery. If the censor's stamp will carry into Canada a letter from the front, I do not see why that letter should not go to its destination just as readily with that censor's stamp on it and without postage stamps on it as my letter goes from the House of Commons with my frank on it. Moreover, putting the stamp on the iso-ldiers' letters involves time and trouble. The minister says that the placing of stamps upon these letters does not involve an increase in the revenues of Canada.
It is a waste of stamps.
I would like to be sure of that because I have an idea that the revenues of Canada are increased to that extent. The minister, however, may know about the matter.

Possibly the method intimated by the minister would be the best one, because I think the whole trouble is due to red tape in the department, and the people have been paying for red tape. The House will anxiously await the solution of this trouble, which to anybody who has anything to do with the postal service in the Old Country so far as the Canadian soldiers are concerned, is certainly a mystery. For that reason I suggest that some other item be taken up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
These' soldiers' letters come together as soldiers' letters, and the man in this country who receives the bundle knows that they are soldiers' letters, but if he sent them off to all their destinations, when one reached the postmaster who would have to deliver it, he would not know it was a soldier's letter, and he would hold it back until double postage was paid. It is only to avoid that difficulty that the stamps are put on. I
understand a system is being sought to be arrived at by which those letters will individually when they are sent from the other side, be stamped as being soldiers' letters. When that comes to be done, of course, it would not be necessary for us to put stamps on them when they reached here. It is only quite recently that the British authorities have undertaken to consent to that system. Until we have a system of that kind identifying a soldier's letter, something has to be done with it to ensure that the recipient would not be held up for additional postage when the letter arrived with nothing on it to show that the postage had been paid, and what was thought the simplest way to show that the postage was paid was to put stamps on it when it arrived in Canada.

I suppose we must accept that reason. Any letters that I have received from soldiers overseas have been marked "on active service" or something of that kind. There is certainly a mark on every letter coming from a soldier to indicate that it is a soldier's letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Some of the letters are marked and some are not. Of course, one could separate all those that bear marks from those that do not and put stamps on those that have no mark and not put stamps on the 'others, but inasmuch as many of them are not marked, it was thought the simplest way to put stamps on them all. *

Are there any well defined regulations or rules of the department by which people in any portion of the country can obtain rural mail service? I was told some years ago that if 50 per cent of all the residents along a certain route or road would subscribe for the boxes and agree to become patrons of the rural mail service they would obtain that as a matter of right. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that where 50 per cent of the people interested make a request a rural mail service is established.

Within the last year or two I have received many complaints, some of which I have forwarded to the department, that those regulations are not lived up to at all, and that the only way the people can get rural mail service is by putting their request through a political organization. In my own constituency the bribe is notoriously put forward that if you will do certain things we will give you a rural mail delivery. I think I am safe in

saying that if 90 per cent of the people in certain districts signed a petition asking for a rural mail delivery they would not get it unless they put their request through the proper political channel. That is the way in which the matter works out. I have not bothered the department very much about the matter, but I have felt a great many times that w'hen these estimates were up I would like to ask the question. I intended to do so last year, but when these estimates went through I was busy at another place in the city. I am glad to have the assurance from my hon. friend to-night that, as a matter of right, 50 per cent of the people living along a certain route can demand the boxes, and I shall have great pleasure in notifying many 'people in my constituency to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not in my knowledge, nor in that of the deputy minister, what representations have been made as to what is necessary in order to get a rural mail service, but I am told by the deputy minister who locates the rural mail routes that he has never had political influence of any kind brought to bear on him in connection with the matter, and that it has been dealt with on the principle which I have just mentioned. That is all the information I have on the subject.

The deputy minister does not know what takes place in the local communities. I have known the deputy minister for a long time, and I kncriv he possesses a great deal of knowledge, but there are taking place around the post office inspector's department, and many places in the different provinces many things of which the deputy minister knows nothing. I assure my hon. friend that what I have described is the practice, but having his assurance to-night, I hope we shall be able' to get rid of that little difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The deputy minister assures me that the routes are laid out in this way, and that the political influence that is talked of has never in any way reached the man who allocates the postal routes. The only conclusion one can draw is that somebody must have misrepresented the matter.

I will bring the thing to a head in a very short time. We will send in an application, and it won't go through the political end of the constituency either, or through the inspector's office, but straight to the deputy minister with ample

evidence that 50 per cent of the people want the accommodation.
Are forms furnished by the department to people who desire to petition for a rural mail route?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Is an affidavit required as to 50 per cent of the inhabitants wanting the accommodation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The deputy tells me it has not been the practice to require an affidavit. The applications may. be made directly to the department or to the inspector. Where they are made through the inspector he is in a position to know, I suppose, whether the petitioners form 50 per cent of the population.

I know that within ten miles of my home a rural mail route was established in a section that was formerly served by a post office. One route was cut off entirely, and the people along it are without mail accommodation at all. I do not know whether this is a case of politics or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member will be good enough to furnish me with the facts I shall be glad to look into the matter.
I was just drawing it to the attention of the minister in that way.

What are the considerations that govern in the establishment of these mail routes? What are the limitations as to the number of people to be served? I know of one or two places myself where I should very much like to see a rural mail delivery route provided, but I am not quite sure that the route is long enough. How many miles long has it to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am informed that there never has been determined an absolute limit below which a route would not be established, but in practice it is not usual to establish a route longer than 20 miles or for a shorter distance than 10 or 12 miles.	As to population,
routes, have been established where the number of people to be served was as low as 25, but that is not usual. I understand that no limits have been fixed as to the length of route or the number of people to be served. The deputy informs me that the department has tried to meet every request for the establishment of a mail route where 50 per cent of the people interested were agreed in asking for it, and where

the length of route and number of people made it at all reasonable.

I was asked a question yesterday which I was unable to answer. Can public documents of this House be mailed free by members of Parliament from any post office in Canada? It would be interesting to know, for instance, in view of the election, if a member could mail a copy of Hansard containing his speech in an open letter from any post office in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that the franking privilege is limited to the House of Commons Post Office.
I understood that official publications could go free from any post office in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that members of Parliament have the right of mailing public documents free from their home post office.
" Is the minister quite sure of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am making the statement on the assurance of the deputy minister. ' My own impression was that the franking privilege was limited to correspondence from Ottawa. Tihe deputy minister informs me that while some distinction is made in regard to public documents, it would not be quite safe to take as positive the answer he gave me a moment ago, but I shall have it verified and let my hon. friend know.
The question was put to me as regards Hansard. Could a member send 100 copies of his speech, for instance, free from his home post office?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The deputy minister informs me that Hansard is not quite what b,e had in mind when speaking of public documents. Hansard, at all events, would have to be mailed from here to go free.

Some time ago a petition was forwarded to the department from the inhabitants of Scotch Hill, in the county of Inverness, asking for the removal of the post office from its present site to the main road.^ Where the post office is now, there are only two mail days a week, and if the post office were removed to the main road the people could get their mail daily, and the department would be saved the cost of carrying the mail to the present site. The petition was signed by every inhabitant
in the district, irrespective of party, except the person who has charge of the post office. I want to know what has been done with that petition, which was forwarded to the department about two months ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall make inquiries and be glad to give the hon. member the information.

Shortly after sending the petition forward, I had a communication from some parties down there, and on making inquiries at the department I was informed that they were awaiting a report from the post office inspector. That report, I presume, is now in the department, and I should like to know what decision has been arrived at.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The deputy minister does not recall at the moment.

I had a communication from some officer in the department-I do not know his name. He said the prayer of the petition was not granted. What I want to call the attention of the minister to particularly is the fairness of the demand of those people, and I cannot understand why their request was disregarded. They wanted to get a daily mail, and by granting their request the department would have saved a matter of $70 or $80 a year, and at this time when money is so scarce it is difficult to me to see why the request was refused. I would ask the minister to be kind enough to give me some information on the subject before the estimates are passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will be glad to look into the matter, and inform my hon. friend as to the result of my inquiry.

I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that Hansard is . "printed by J. de L. Tache, Printer to the King's Most Excellent Majesty," and would appear to be a public document entitled to be sent free through the post by members. Will the minister kindly clear up the matter so that we may know where we stand with regard to the mailing of Hansard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I will ask the deputy minister to distribute copies of the regulations.

I wbuld like to ask the minister, for some information in Tegard to the St, Pierre-Miquelon mails. They used to be conveyed from Halifax to North Sydney by rail, then placed on board the steamer for St. Pierre. This steamer runs

from St. Pierre to Halifax, calling at North Sydney, and when she returns from Halifax to St. Pierre she also calls at North Sydney and there receives all the Canadian mail. The mails are brought from Halifax to North Sydney by rail, unloaded there on trucks, and brought into the post office, where there is very poor accommodation for them. The place is comparatively small, and these mails fill it up so that you can hardly move around. After they have been there for some time they are re-trucked from the post office and put aboard the boat. This was the custom, and I believe it is still carried on. I could never understand why those mails were not put aboard the steamer at Halifax. Not a moment of time is gained by sending them by rail to North Sydney because there they have to wait for the boat. I brought this matter before the Postmaster General some years ago, and was told some change had been made, but so far as I know nothing has been done. The people of North Sydney protest very strongly against the practice, because it results in filling the post office up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It certainly does seem as if thiat were a very reasonable request.
I will look into it. I understand the hon. member is not quite sure as to whether that system still prevails.
I think it does.

I would like the minister to tell me how the amount of $3,519,932 for mail service by railway is made up.
I take it that is the amount which is paid to the different railway companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the total
amount paid to the railways for mail service.
On what basis is it arrived at?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are different contracts with different companies, and that the services are paid for at so rnuqh per running mile.
How much per running mile?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They are paid at the
rate of 16 cents per running mile for a car, and nine cents per half oar, and that in certain places where a baggage oar is supplied they are paid four cents per running mile.	'
Is not that quite an increase over what it was a few years ago? TMr. McKenzie. 1

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was an increase made two years ago. The rates were then readjusted. I understand the arrangement did not really result in an increase. The difference is they are now paid per running mile, whereas previously they were paid per track mile.
Then, if they carry two miails a day they would really get double what they were getting when they were being paid by the track mile?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not quite follow that. I understand that on the track mile system the post office used any car that was available and paid for the number of track miles, while they now have a car especially purchased and pay for the number of miles that the car runs.
What was the percentage of increase to the railway companies as a result of the readjustment a few years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand it was approximately $1,000,000 per yeaT.
Before the war broke out?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

I wish to bring up a complaint with reference to unsatisfactory mail service on the Intercolonial in a very large portion of my constituency, particularly during the winter. For years a train leaving St. John at seven a.m. has connected at Moncton with the Maritime Express during the winter, although it runs on to Truro in the summer. The Maritime Express is supposed to take the mail on from Moncton. If, as frequently happens in winter, the Maritime Express is more than two hours late, a special is run through from Moncton. But on that special they do not carry mails or papers and all the eastern section of Westmorland county from Moncton down is deprived of mail service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall ask to have the matter investigated. It seems only reasonable that we should take advantage of the special train.

I have here a memorial by certain railway mail clerks. It appears that railway mail clerks operating west of Sudbury receive a provisional allowance of $15 a month in addition to the regular pay. Clerks operating east of Sudbury do not receive that. According to the memorial placed in my hands, the eastern men discussed this matter with the late lamented

Mr. Casgrain shortly before he died, and they say that they had made good progress in their negotiations with him, that he was much impressed with their story and that something was about to be done. Owing to the death of Mr. Casgrain and several changes in- the Postmaster Generalship that have occurred since, nothing has been done. They ask that all railway clerks in the eastern division be placed upon the same footing as those in the West. I am requested by the clerk of the association to bring this matter to the notice of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be glad to consider it. The payment of a special 'allowance to western employees is not confined to the post office. Owing to the high cost of living in the West, many departments have granted an extra allowance to employees there. As to the particular case, I presume that the memorial will be brought to my knowledge and I shall be able to give it consideration. In the allowance that we propose to make to employees on salaries of $1,000 or under there will be some step in the direction of equalization, because it is contemplated to give a larger allowance to the eastern men- who have not presently this additional amount than it is contemplated to give to western men. That would not apply to all railway mail clerks inasmuch as the salaries of some of them are larger than $1,000.

This memorial says
that in April, 1914, an Act put through by the Postmaster General, granting certain concessions to those clerks in the eastern division, but it went to the Senate, and, being mixed up with other Acts that were defeated, this Act, while in itself not objectionable, fell by the way with the other Acts, and nothing was done. This is evidently not a new matter, and perhaps the knowledge of that Act having passed through the House would help the minister in reaching a conclusion in regard to it.

I would like to take advantage of the presence of the d-eputy minister to ask a question in regard to the postmastership at. Dorchester, N.B. The office became vacant recently. Has an appointment been made, and if so, who is the present official?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand it has not been filled.

I have been asked to obtain some information from the department in connection with the postmastership
in the town of Stellarton, in the county of Pictou. Some -questions were asked not long ago as to who the postmaster was, and I understand the answer was that a man by the name of William G. Miller was postmaster, the former postmaster, Alexander Inglis, having been dismissed, but my information is that Inglis is still acting postmaster, and it is regarded as peculiar that the gentleman who was referred to in answer to questions, as the dismissed official is -still performing the duties of postmaster, while the real postmaster is William G. Miller. Is there any explanation, first, as to why this man- was dismissed, and, if dismissed, why was the regularly appointed official not installed in office, and why is he not discharging the duties of the office at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am informed that the reason why he was dismissed was that his , performance of the duties was not satisfactory. He was insubordinate and negligent, and more particularly, I think, in the matter of answering correspondence and giving information. At all events, he was dismissed, -and Mr. Miller was appointed, but the actual transfer of the post office has been delayed, by reason of the fact that it was necessary to make certain alterations in Mr. Miller's establishment, to adapt it to the business of the post office. Tho-s-e alterations are nearly completed, and, pending their completion, it was not convenient that Mr. Miller -should carry on the business instead of Mr. -Inglis. Mr. -In-glis has been acting postmaster, pending the alterations in Miller's premises. It is expected that in a week or two the new premises will be in proper order.

I did not expect the
.minister to have any information about the premises, but I -am told the whole store owned by Mr. MilleT is now rented by the Government. It is a -small store, but rented at rather a g-ood price, namely $600 a year, by th-e Government. As the minister is -aware that some changes are being made in this building, perhaps he could tell us whether the Government rented th-e building, or is it in that building that changes are being -made for the post office?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Po-st Office Department made the usual -allowance to Mr. Miller for rental, hut, in view of the nature o-f the premises be is furnishing, the Public Works Department is making a certain addition to that allowance, bringing the total up t-o $50 a month, which is paid to him as rental.

Does the minister
kno-w what the Public Works Department want this for?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They want it for the
business of the department.
Is the minister satisfied with the night's work?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, very well satisfied.

There are some other
items in the supplementary estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I have some items.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, there will he items in the supplementary estimates, but that, covers the main items.

Does the Minister of
Labour intend proceeding with his items to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Yes, they will not take very long.
Fair wages and inspection officers, $15,000.

I would like to
ask the minister if the findings made, by Mr. O'Connor are to be referred to a judge for further inquiry?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The matter has not
yet been fully determined. My hon. friend will remember that, in the order in council passed November last, provision is made for a further examination under the directions of the Minister of Labour, who is authorized to appoint an examiner, and to confer upon him power to examine books and witnesses under oath, and all that sort of thing. Whether a further investigation will proceed under that clause of the order in council or otherwise, I am not in a position to say definitely, but there will be a further investigation.	*

I did not make
myself plain. What I meant to inquire of him was whether his Teport, covering the matters of bacon and foodstuffs, is to be the subject of an investigation by some judicial tribunal. There is some intimation of that in the press to-day. If there is to be such an inquiry, has a judge been appointed yet to conduct it?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I think I understood
what the hon. gentleman asked. What I said was that it had not been determined yet whether there would be- a further inquiry or investigation under that order in council. There will be' a further investigation.
[Mr. Doherty.!
Will there be an appeal from that investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
No telling what the
future may bring forth. Perhaps I ought to makq a little explanation as to a misunderstanding concerning that report. Questionnaires were sent out to those having cold storages in Canada, somewhere about a hundred, I think, just as we had sent out questionnaires to dealers in coal.
What are questionnaires?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is a name given to a set of questions. Take the matter of bacon, for instance; the first question was as to the quantity of bacon on hand on a certain date. The next question was with regard to the cost of the bacon laid down in cold storage, including freight and unloading charges. The questions were answered satisfactorily. The next question was: what was the storage, overhead, and delivery cost. One or two of the firms said: " we cannot answer these questions; we are not in a position to give you the particulars." Hon. gentlemen will see at once that in the case of bacon that is sold in Liverpool that the delivery charges would be a very important matter. No answer was given to that question by the firm about which there has been so much talk during the last few days. In his report, Mr. O'Connor does not profess to deal with net profits; he deals with what is known in economics as margins. He pointed out the gross profit, that is the difference between the cost of the bacon and its selling price. Margin is made up of the different items of cost, delivery charges, overhead and cold storage charges -which the firm failed to give us. In a day or two after the report was filed these items of margin, the cost of delivery, storage and overhead charges were all provided and published in the Citizen and other newspapers.

Then what is the purpose of having a further inquiry by a judge? Why should not Mr. O'Connor make a further explanation of his report, having obtained from the firms investigated information which they failed to give to him upon request earlier in the proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
It is thought desirable that the information should be got by the department through some special officer- not necessarily a judge, though that has not been determined. Uuder the order in council we have power to send a man out

who may examine the books of the company and any witnesses under oath that it may think it desirable to call, with a view to ascertaining without any doubt what the net profits of this particular concern were within a certain period.

The Government seems to have established a peculiar system under which these examinations go on indefinitely. You appoint a commissioner to make certain inquiries according to the best of his ability. Perhaps his report is not quite satisfactory to the party whose affairs are investigated. Accordingly, that party raises a howl and makes a lot of noise, the effect of his noise being proportionate to the influence he has with the department or with the Government, and, in some degree, to the size of the interests that he represents. Then another commis-
11 p.m. sioner is- appointed to investigate the first commission. If the second commissioner is not orthodox in his report, the first may say: This report is not fair to me; I did the best I could; I furnished the facts and gave good reasons for the conclusions to which I came. Over my head you have appointed a judge who does not agree with me. I want to investigate him; he is not right; he is not fair. And then it goes on-ad infinitum. There is -an old saying, well known to the Minister of Labour, that it is in the interest of the state that litigation should end. The minister should tell his officials that when they make a report upon a matter of this kind, the report will be final; that the first investigation or finding of a properly constituted court must be considered as final. If that is done, the public will know that when a report is filed, that is the end of the matter. The principle established now seems to be that of waiting a certain number of years after the filing of the first report for a further report on the subject. Has the minister any particular policy in his department in that regard? Is there any statute of limitation which he regards as applying to these investigating commissions?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: In his report Mr. O'Connor points out that the information is not complete and he asks that an expert accountant be employed to make a further investigation. This was done before the William Davies Company ever saw or heard of the report., I quite agree with my hon. friend that it would have been better that further investigation by an expert accountant should have been made before the report was published. But the further investigation is not to be an investigation of Mr. O'Connor's work, whether it was right or not right; it is the further investigation under order in council- as recommended by Mr. O'Connor in his report.
Do I understand that the minister thinks he was premature in submitting the incomplete report to the House?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I admit frankly that it would have been better to have had an investigation by an expert accountant first.
Perhaps "it would have been better" is a mild way of saying that, it was a grievous mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Characterize it as you please.
Mr. A. ~K. MACLEAN: Mr. O'Connor made reports also with respect to coal, sugar and other commodities. Was his investigation complete in this or should further inquiry have been made? Perhaps these reports also were defective; perhaps he lacked some information which was not supplied by the parties interested. It is a very serious matter if the inquiry was not complete or the information given not reliable.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The answers sent in concerning anthracite coal and sugar were satisfactory; it was not considered necessary to make any further investigation by an expert accountant. But my hon. friend will realize that the investigations never cease. We are getting monthly reports from all the leading coal dealers and sugar dealers and cold storage people in Canada concerning the quantity of goods in storage and the amounts bought and sold during the month in question. In that sense, therefore, the investigation continues right along, going back to the year 1913. There is an immense amount of work connected with it. The inquiry will continue right along in that sense.

The minister must be
unconscious of what is going on. He says that it has not yet been decided whether there is going to be a further investigation by Mr. O'Connor.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I did not say a further investigation by Mr. O'Connor; I said a further investigation under the order in council, by an expert accountant.

Let me read what the Prime Minister says in a telegram to the William Davies Company. A despatch from Toronto states:

This morning, the William Davies Company received a reply from Sir Robert Borden to the telegram sent the morning after the publication of the O'Connor report. Sir Robert's telegram says:
"I think it desirable that an investigation into the whole matter raised by Mr. O'Connor's report should be made by a competent judicial officer. This course I propose to direct." (Signed) "R. L. Borden."

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Is the word "judicial" there?
Yes-"by a competent judicial officer." The minister was not aware of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I have seen the telegram.

But the minister did
not know the word "judicial" was in it;

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I read the whole telegram, but I do not think the term "judicial officer" is necessarily confined to a judge.

What is the meaning
of the term "judicial officer " if it does not mean a judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I do not think it is
confined to a judge.

What class of officers
would it cover?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I do not propose entering into a discussion as to the definition of the term.

A lawyer of ten years' standing might come upder that.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Does the minister make any inquiry as to the wages paid by contractors who have large contracts with the Home Government for supplying war munitions?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I understand that the Imperial Munitions Board does not insert in any of its contracts what is known as a detailed schedule giving the schedule of wages or the general fair-wage clause; but when any complaints are made to us-and there have been a few, although not many -we have made an inquiry and then taken the matter up with the chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board, and he has gone, in at least one case, sb far as to cancel the contract because the contractor refused to pay the wages that we found were current in the neighbourhood and which we thought should be paid. When any complaint is made regarding wages we make inquiries just as we do in the case of contracts let by our Government.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty, the House adjourned at 11.12 p.m.
Saturday, July 21, 1917.
